{"path":"arrow-libs/core/arrow-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/core/Either.kt","prefix":"@file:JvmMultifileClass\n@file:JvmName(\"EitherKt\")\n@file:OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)\n\npackage arrow.core\n\nimport arrow.core.Either.Left\nimport arrow.core.Either.Right\nimport arrow.core.Either.Right.Companion.unit\nimport arrow.core.raise.Raise\nimport arrow.core.raise.either\nimport kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts\nimport kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind\nimport kotlin.contracts.contract\nimport kotlin.experimental.ExperimentalTypeInference\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmMultifileClass\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmName\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmStatic\n\npublic typealias EitherNel<E, A> = Either<NonEmptyList<E>, A>\n\n/**\n * <!--- TEST_NAME EitherKnitTest -->\n *\n * In day-to-day programming, it is fairly common to find ourselves writing functions that can fail.\n * For instance, querying a service may result in a connection issue, or some unexpected JSON response.\n *\n * To communicate these errors, it has become common practice to throw exceptions; however,\n * exceptions are not tracked in any way, shape, or form by the compiler. To see what\n * kind of exceptions (if any) a function may throw, we have to dig through the source code.\n * Then, to handle these exceptions, we have to make sure we catch them at the call site. This\n * all becomes even more unwieldy when we try to compose exception-throwing procedures.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * //sampleStart\n * val throwsSomeStuff: (Int) -> Double = {x -> x.toDouble()}\n * val throwsOtherThings: (Double) -> String = {x -> x.toString()}\n * val moreThrowing: (String) -> List<String> = {x -> listOf(x)}\n * val magic: (Int) -> List<String> = { x ->\n *   val y = throwsSomeStuff(x)\n *   val z = throwsOtherThings(y)\n *   moreThrowing(z)\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println (\"magic = $magic\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-01.kt -->\n *\n * Assume we happily throw exceptions in our code. Looking at the types of the functions above, any could throw a number of exceptions -- we do not know. When we compose, exceptions from any of the constituent\n * functions can be thrown. Moreover, they may throw the same kind of exception\n * (e.g., `IllegalArgumentException`) and, thus, it gets tricky tracking exactly where an exception came from.\n *\n * How then do we communicate an error? By making it explicit in the data type we return.\n *\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * val left: Either<String, Int> =\n * //sampleStart\n *  Either.Left(\"Something went wrong\")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(left)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-02.kt -->\n *\n * Because `Either` is right-biased, it is possible to define a Monad instance for it.\n *\n * Since we only ever want the computation to continue in the case of [Right] (as captured by the right-bias nature),\n * we fix the left type parameter and leave the right one free.\n *\n * So, the map and flatMap methods are right-biased:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val right: Either<String, Int> = Either.Right(5)\n * val value = right.flatMap{ Either.Right(it + 1) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val left: Either<String, Int> = Either.Left(\"Something went wrong\")\n * val value = left.flatMap{ Either.Right(it + 1) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-04.kt -->\n *\n * ## Using Either instead of exceptions\n *\n * As a running example, we will have a series of functions that will:\n *\n * * Parse a string into an integer\n * * Calculate the reciprocal\n * * Convert the reciprocal into a string\n *\n * Using exception-throwing code, we could write something like this:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun parse(s: String): Int =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) s.toInt()\n *   else throw NumberFormatException(\"$s is not a valid integer.\")\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Double =\n *   if (i == 0) throw IllegalArgumentException(\"Cannot take reciprocal of 0.\")\n *   else 1.0 / i\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-05.kt -->\n *\n * Instead, let's make the fact that some of our functions can fail explicit in the return type.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n * import arrow.core.left\n * import arrow.core.right\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * // Either Style\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException(\"$s is not a valid integer.\"))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException(\"Cannot take reciprocal of 0.\"))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap { reciprocal(it) }.map { stringify(it) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-06.kt -->\n *\n * These calls to `parse` return a [Left] and [Right] value\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException(\"$s is not a valid integer.\"))\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val notANumber = parse(\"Not a number\")\n * val number2 = parse(\"2\")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"notANumber = $notANumber\")\n *  println(\"number2 = $number2\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-07.kt -->\n *\n * Now, using combinators like `flatMap` and `map`, we can compose our functions together.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException(\"$s is not a valid integer.\"))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException(\"Cannot take reciprocal of 0.\"))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val magic0 = magic(\"0\")\n * val magic1 = magic(\"1\")\n * val magicNotANumber = magic(\"Not a number\")\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"magic0 = $magic0\")\n *  println(\"magic1 = $magic1\")\n *  println(\"magicNotANumber = $magicNotANumber\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-08.kt -->\n *\n * In the following exercise, we pattern-match on every case in which the `Either` returned by `magic` can be in.\n * Note the `when` clause in the [Left] - the compiler will complain if we leave that out because it knows that,\n * given the type `Either[Exception, String]`, there can be inhabitants of [Left] that are not\n * `NumberFormatException` or `IllegalArgumentException`. You should also notice that we are using\n * [SmartCast](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/typecasts.html#smart-casts) for accessing [Left] and [Right]\n * values.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<NumberFormatException, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(NumberFormatException(\"$s is not a valid integer.\"))\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<IllegalArgumentException, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(IllegalArgumentException(\"Cannot take reciprocal of 0.\"))\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Exception, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = magic(\"2\")\n * val value = when(x) {\n *   is Either.Left -> when (x.value) {\n *     is NumberFormatException -> \"Not a number!\"\n *     is IllegalArgumentException -> \"Can't take reciprocal of 0!\"\n *     else -> \"Unknown error\"\n *   }\n *   is Either.Right -> \"Got reciprocal: ${x.value}\"\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-09.kt -->\n *\n * Instead of using exceptions as our error value, let's instead enumerate explicitly the things that\n * can go wrong in our program.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n * //sampleStart\n * // Either with ADT Style\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *   object NotANumber : Error()\n *   object NoZeroReciprocal : Error()\n * }\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<Error, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(Error.NotANumber)\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<Error, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(Error.NoZeroReciprocal)\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Error, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{reciprocal(it)}.map{ stringify(it) }\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-10.kt -->\n *\n * For our little module, we enumerate any and all errors that can occur. Then, instead of using\n * exception classes as error values, we use one of the enumerated cases. Now, when we pattern match,\n * we are able to comphrensively handle failure without resulting in an `else` branch; moreover,\n * since Error is sealed, no outside code can add additional subtypes that we might fail to handle.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.flatMap\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *  object NotANumber : Error()\n *  object NoZeroReciprocal : Error()\n * }\n *\n * fun parse(s: String): Either<Error, Int> =\n *   if (s.matches(Regex(\"-?[0-9]+\"))) Either.Right(s.toInt())\n *   else Either.Left(Error.NotANumber)\n *\n * fun reciprocal(i: Int): Either<Error, Double> =\n *   if (i == 0) Either.Left(Error.NoZeroReciprocal)\n *   else Either.Right(1.0 / i)\n *\n * fun stringify(d: Double): String = d.toString()\n *\n * fun magic(s: String): Either<Error, String> =\n *   parse(s).flatMap{ reciprocal(it) }.map{ stringify(it) }\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = magic(\"2\")\n * val value = when(x) {\n *   is Either.Left -> when (x.value) {\n *     is Error.NotAN","middle":"umber -> \"Not a number!\"\n *     is Error.NoZeroReciprocal -> \"Can't take reciprocal of 0!\"\n *   }\n *   is Either.Right -> \"Got reciprocal: ${x.value}\"\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-11.kt -->\n *\n * ## Either.catch exceptions\n *\n * Sometimes you do need to interact with code that can potentially throw exceptions. In such cases, you should mitigate the possibility that an exception can be thrown. You can do so by using the `catch` function.\n *\n * Example:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun potentialThrowingCode(): String = throw RuntimeException(\"Blow up!\")\n *\n * suspend fun makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects(): Either<Error, String> =\n *   Either.catch { potentialThrowingCode() }.mapLeft { Error.SpecificError }\n * //sampleEnd\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   println(\"makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects().isLeft() = ${makeSureYourLogicDoesNotHaveSideEffects().isLeft()}\")\n * }\n *\n * sealed class Error {\n *   object SpecificError : Error()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-12.kt -->\n *\n * ## Syntax\n *\n * Either can also map over the [Left] value with `mapLeft`, which is similar to map, but applies on left instances.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val r : Either<Int, Int> = Either.Right(7)\n * val rightMapLeft = r.mapLeft {it + 1}\n * val l: Either<Int, Int> = Either.Left(7)\n * val leftMapLeft = l.mapLeft {it + 1}\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"rightMapLeft = $rightMapLeft\")\n *  println(\"leftMapLeft = $leftMapLeft\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-13.kt -->\n *\n * `Either<A, B>` can be transformed to `Either<B,A>` using the `swap()` method.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either.Left\n * import arrow.core.Either\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val r: Either<String, Int> = Either.Right(7)\n * val swapped = r.swap()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"swapped = $swapped\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-14.kt -->\n *\n * For using Either's syntax on arbitrary data types.\n * This will make possible to use the `left()`, `right()`, `getOrElse()` methods:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.right\n *\n * val right7 =\n * //sampleStart\n *   7.right()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(right7)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-15.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.left\n *\n *  val leftHello =\n * //sampleStart\n *  \"hello\".left()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(leftHello)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-16.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.left\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val x = \"hello\".left()\n * val value = x.getOrElse { \"$it world!\" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-either-17.kt -->\n *\n * Another operation is `fold`. {"path":"arrow-libs/core/arrow-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/core/raise/Effect.kt","prefix":"@file:JvmMultifileClass\n@file:JvmName(\"RaiseKt\")\n@file:OptIn(ExperimentalTypeInference::class)\npackage arrow.core.raise\n\nimport kotlin.experimental.ExperimentalTypeInference\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmMultifileClass\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmName\n\n/**\n * [Effect] represents a function of `suspend Raise<R>.() -> A`, that short-circuit with a value of `R` or `Throwable`, or completes with a value of `A`.\n *\n * So [Effect] is defined by `suspend fun <B> fold(recover: suspend (Throwable) -> B, resolve: suspend (R) -> B, transform: suspend (A) -> B): B`,\n * to map all values of `R`, `Throwable` and `A` to a value of `B`.\n *\n * <!--- TOC -->\n\n      * [Writing a program with Effect<R, A>](#writing-a-program-with-effect<r-a>)\n      * [Handling errors](#handling-errors)\n        * [recover](#recover)\n        * [catch](#catch)\n      * [Structured Concurrency](#structured-concurrency)\n        * [Arrow Fx Coroutines](#arrow-fx-coroutines)\n          * [parZip](#parzip)\n          * [parTraverse](#partraverse)\n          * [raceN](#racen)\n          * [bracketCase / Resource](#bracketcase--resource)\n        * [KotlinX](#kotlinx)\n          * [withContext](#withcontext)\n          * [async](#async)\n          * [launch](#launch)\n          * [Strange edge cases](#strange-edge-cases)\n\n * <!--- END -->\n *\n * ## Writing a program with Effect<R, A>\n *\n * Let's write a small program to read a file from disk, and instead of having the program work exception based we want to\n * turn it into a polymorphic type-safe program.\n *\n * We'll start by defining a small function that accepts a [String], and does some simply validation to check that the path\n * is not empty. If the path is empty, we want to program to result in `EmptyPath`. So we're immediately going to see how\n * we can raise an error of any arbitrary type `R` by using the function `raise`. The name `raise` comes raising an intterupt, or\n * changing, especially unexpectedly, away from the computation and finishing the `Continuation` with `R`.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensureNotNull\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensure\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * object EmptyPath\n *\n * fun readFile(path: String): Effect<EmptyPath, Unit> = effect {\n *   if (path.isEmpty()) raise(EmptyPath) else Unit\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * Here we see how we can define an `Effect<R, A>` which has `EmptyPath` for the raise type `R`, and `Unit` for the success type `A`.\n *\n * Patterns like validating a [Boolean] is very common, and the [Effect] DSL offers utility functions like [kotlin.require]\n * and [kotlin.requireNotNull]. They're named [ensure] and [ensureNotNull] to avoid conflicts with the `kotlin` namespace.\n * So let's rewrite the function from above to use the DSL instead.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * fun readFile2(path: String?): Effect<EmptyPath, Unit> = effect {\n *   ensureNotNull(path) { EmptyPath }\n *   ensure(path.isNotEmpty()) { EmptyPath }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-01.kt -->\n *\n * Now that we have the path, we can read from the `File` and return it as a domain model `Content`.\n * We also want to take a look at what exceptions reading from a file might occur `FileNotFoundException` & `SecurityError`,\n * so lets make some domain errors for those too. Grouping them as a sealed interface is useful since that way we can resolve *all* errors in a type safe manner.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.Ior\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.core.raise.toEither\n * import arrow.core.raise.toIor\n * import arrow.core.raise.toOption\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensureNotNull\n * import arrow.core.raise.ensure\n * import io.kotest.matchers.collections.shouldNotBeEmpty\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import io.kotest.matchers.types.shouldBeInstanceOf\n * import java.io.File\n * import java.io.FileNotFoundException\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * @JvmInline\n * value class Content(val body: List<String>)\n *\n * sealed interface FileError\n * @JvmInline value class SecurityError(val msg: String?) : FileError\n * @JvmInline value class FileNotFound(val path: String) : FileError\n * object EmptyPath : FileError {\n *   override fun toString() = \"EmptyPath\"\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * We can finish our function, but we need to refactor the return type from `Unit` to `Content` and the error type from `EmptyPath` to `FileError`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * fun readFile(path: String?): Effect<FileError, Content> = effect {\n *   ensureNotNull(path) { EmptyPath }\n *   ensure(path.isNotEmpty()) { EmptyPath }\n *   try {\n *     val lines = File(path).readLines()\n *     Content(lines)\n *   } catch (e: FileNotFoundException) {\n *     raise(FileNotFound(path))\n *   } catch (e: SecurityException) {\n *     raise(SecurityError(e.message))\n *   }\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * The `readFile` function defines a `suspend fun` that will return:\n *\n * - the `Content` of a given `path`\n * - a `FileError`\n * - An unexpected fatal error (`OutOfMemoryException`)\n *\n * Since these are the properties of our `Effect` function, we can turn it into a value.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun main() {\n *    readFile(\"\").toEither() shouldBe Either.Left(EmptyPath)\n *    readFile(\"gradle.properties\").toIor() shouldBe Ior.Left(FileNotFound(\"gradle.properties\"))\n *    readFile(\"README.MD\").toOption { None } shouldBe None\n *\n *    readFile(\"build.gradle.kts\").fold({ _: FileError -> null }, { it })\n *      .shouldBeInstanceOf<Content>()\n *       .body.shouldNotBeEmpty()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-02.kt -->\n *\n * The functions above are available out of the box, but it's easy to define your own extension functions in terms\n * of `fold`. Implementing the `toEither()` operator is as simple as:\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.core.identity\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun <R, A> Effect<R, A>.toEither(): Either<R, A> =\n *   fold({ Either.Left(it) }) { Either.Right(it) }\n *\n * suspend fun <A> Effect<None, A>.toOption(): Option<A> =\n *   fold(::identity) { Some(it) }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-03.kt -->\n *\n * Adding your own syntax to `Raise<R>` is not advised, yet, but will be easy once \"Multiple Receivers\" become available.\n *\n * ```\n * context(Raise<R>)\n * suspend fun <R, A> Either<R, A>.bind(): A =\n *   when (this) {\n *     is Either.Left -> raise(value)\n *     is Either.Right -> value\n *   }\n *\n * context(Raise<None>)\n * fun <A> Option<A>.bind(): A =\n *   fold({ raise(it) }, ::identity)\n * ```\n *\n * ## Handling errors\n *\n * An Effect<R, A> has 2 error channels: `Throwable` and `R`\n * There are two separate handlers to transform either of the error channels.\n *\n * - `recover` to handle, and transform any error of type `R`.\n * - `catch` to handle, and transform and error of type `Throwable`.\n *\n * ### recover\n *\n * `recover` handles the error of type `R`,\n * by providing a new value of type `A`, raising a different error of type `E`, or throwing an exception.\n *\n * Let's take a look at some examples:\n *\n * We define a `val failed` of type `Effect<String, Int>`, that represents a failed effect with value \"failed\".\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.Effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.recover\n * import arrow.core.raise.catch\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * val failed: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   effect { raise(\"failed\") }\n * ```\n *\n * We can `recover` the failure, and resolve it by providing a default value of `-1` or the length of the `error: String`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { -1 }\n *\n * val resolved: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { it.length }\n * ```\n *\n * As you can see the resulting `error` is now of type `Nothing`, since we did not raise any new errors.\n * So our `Effect` knows that no short-circuiting will occur during execution. Awesome!\n * But it can also infer to any other error type that you might want instead, because it's never going to occur.\n * So as you see below, we can even assign our `Effect<Nothing, A>` to `Effect<E, A>`, where `E` can be any type.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default2: Effect<Double, Int> = default\n * val resolved2: Effect<Unit, Int> = resolved\n * ```\n *\n * `recover` also allows us to _change_ the error type when we resolve the error of type `R`.\n * Below we handle our error of `String` and turn it into `List<Char>` using `reversed().toList()`.\n * This is a powerful operation, since it allows us to transform our error types across boundaries or layers.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val newError: Effect<List<Char>, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { str ->\n *     raise(str.reversed().toList())\n *   }\n * ```\n *\n * Finally, since `recover` supports `suspend` we can safely call other `suspend` code and throw `Throwable` into the `suspend` system.\n * This is typically undesired, since you should prefer lifting `Throwable` into typed values of `R` to make them compile-time tracked.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val newException: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   failed.recover { str -> throw RuntimeException(str) }\n * ```\n *\n * ### catch\n *\n * `catch` gives us the same powers as `recover`, but instead of resolving `R` we're recovering from any unexpected `Throwable`.\n * Unexpected, because the expectation is that all `Throwable` get turned into `R` unless it's a fatal/unexpected.\n * This operator is useful when you need to work/wrap foreign code, especially Java SDKs or any code that is heavily based on exceptions.\n *\n * Below we've defined a `foreign` value that represents wrapping a foreign API which might throw `RuntimeException`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val foreign = effect<String, Int> {\n *   throw RuntimeException(\"BOOM!\")\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * We can `catch` to run the effect recovering from any exception,\n * and recover it by providing a default value of `-1` or the length of the [Throwable.message].\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default3: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign.catch { -1 }\n *\n * val resolved3: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign.catch { it.message?.length ?: -1 }\n * ```\n *\n * A big difference with `recover` is that `catch` **cannot** change the error type of `R` because it doesn't resolve it, so it stays unchanged.\n * You can however compose `recover`, and `v` to resolve the error type **and** recover the exception.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default4: Effect<Nothing, Int> =\n *   foreign\n *     .recover<String, Nothing, Int> { -1 }\n *     .catch { -2 }\n * ```\n *\n * `catch` however offers an overload that can _refine the exception_.\n * Let's say you're wrapping some database interactions that might throw `java.sql.SqlException`, or `org.postgresql.util.PSQLException`,\n * then you might only be interested in those exceptions and not `Throwable`. `catch` allows you to install multiple handlers for specific exceptions.\n * If the desired exception is not matched, then it stays in the `suspend` exception channel and will be thrown or recovered at a later point.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * val default5: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   foreign\n *     .catch { _: RuntimeException -> -1 }\n *     .catch { _: java.sql.SQLException -> -2 }\n * ```\n *\n * Finally, since `catch` also supports `suspend` we can safely call other `suspend` code and throw `Throwable` into the `suspend` system.\n * This can be useful if refinement of exceptions is not sufficient, for example in the case of `org.postgresql.util.PSQLException` you might want to\n * check the `SQLState` to check for a `foreign key violation` and rethrow the exception if not matched.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun java.sql.SQLException.isForeignKeyViolation(): Boolean = true\n *\n * val rethrown: Effect<String, Int> =\n *   failed.catch { ex: java.sql.SQLException ->\n *     if(ex.isForeignKeyViolation()) raise(\"foreign key violation\")\n *     else throw ex\n *   }\n * ```\n *\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-04.kt -->\n *\n * Note:\n *  Handling errors can also be done with `try/catch` but this is **not recommended**, it uses `CancellationException` which is used to cancel `Coroutine`s and is advised not to capture in Kotlin.\n *  The `CancellationException` from `Effect` is `RaiseCancellationException`, this a public type, thus can be distinguished from any other `CancellationException` if necessary.\n *\n * ## Structured Concurrency\n *\n * `Effect<R, A>` relies on `kotlin.cancellation.CancellationException` to `raise` error values of type `R` inside the `Continuation` since it effectively cancels/short-circuits it.\n * For this reason `raise` adheres to the same rules as [`Structured Concurrency`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-basics.html#structured-concurrency)\n *\n * Let's overview below how `raise` behaves with the different concurrency builders from Arrow Fx & KotlinX Coroutines.\n * In the examples below we're going to be using a utility to show how _sibling tasks_ get cancelled.\n * The utility function show below called `awaitExitCase` will `never` finish suspending, and completes a `Deferred` with the `ExitCase`.\n * `ExitCase` is a sealed class that can be a value of `Failure(Throwable)`, `Cancelled(CancellationException)`, or `Completed`.\n * Since `awaitExitCase` suspends forever, it can only result in `Cancelled(CancellationException)`.\n *\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.guaranteeCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.parZip\n * import io.kotest.assertions.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import io.kotest.matchers.types.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun <A> awaitExitCase(exit: CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>): A =\n *   guaranteeCase(::awaitCancellation) { exitCase -> exit.complete(exitCase) }\n *\n * ```\n *\n * ### Arrow Fx Coroutines\n * All operators in Arrow Fx Coroutines run in place, so they have no way of leaking `raise`.\n * It's there always safe to compose `effect` with any Arrow Fx combinator. Let's see some small examples below.\n *\n * #### parZip\n *\n * ```kotlin\n *  suspend fun main() {\n *    val error = \"Error\"\n *    val exit = CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>()\n *   effect<String, Int> {\n *     parZip({ awaitExitCase<Int>(exit) }, { raise(error) }) { a: Int, b: Int -> a + b }\n *   }.fold({ it shouldBe error }, { fail(\"Int can never be the result\") })\n *   exit.await().shouldBeTypeOf<ExitCase>()\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-05.kt -->\n *\n * #### parTraverse\n * <!--- INCLUDE\n * import arrow.core.raise.effect\n * import arrow.core.raise.fold\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.ExitCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.guaranteeCase\n * import arrow.fx.coroutines.parMap\n * import io.kotest.assertions.fail\n * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n * import io.kotest.matchers.types.shouldBeTypeOf\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation\n *\n * suspend fun <A> awaitExitCase(exit: CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>): A =\n *  guaranteeCase(::awaitCancellation) { exitCase -> exit.complete(exitCase) }\n *\n * suspend fun <A> CompletableDeferred<A>.getOrNull(): A? =\n *  if (isCompleted) await() else null\n * -->\n * ```kotlin\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   val error = \"Error\"\n *   val exits = (0..3).map { CompletableDeferred<ExitCase>() }\n *   effect<String, List<Unit>> {\n *     (0..4).parMap { index ->\n *       if (index == 4) raise(error)\n *       else awaitExitCase(exits[index])\n *     }\n *   }.fold({ msg -> msg shouldBe error }, { fail(\"Int can never be the result\") })\n *   // It's possible not all parallel task got launched, and in those cases awaitCancellation never ran\n *   exits.forEach { exit -> exit.getOrNull()?.shouldBeTypeOf<ExitCase.Cancelled>() }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-raise-06.kt -->\n *\n * `parTraverse` will launch 5 tasks, for every element in `1..5`.\n * The last task {"path":"arrow-libs/fx/arrow-fx-stm/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/fx/stm/TMVar.kt","prefix":"package arrow.fx.stm\n\npublic fun <A> STM.newTMVar(a: A): TMVar<A> = TMVar<A>(newTVar(Option.Some(a)))\npublic fun <A> STM.newEmptyTMVar(): TMVar<A> = TMVar<A>(newTVar(Option.None))\n\n/**\n * A [TMVar] is a mutable reference that can either be empty or hold a value.\n *\n * The main use for [TMVar] is as a synchronization primitive as it can be used to force other transactions\n *  to wait until a [TMVar] is full.\n *\n * ## Creating a [TMVar]:\n *\n * As usual with [STM] types there are two equal sets of operators for creating them, one that can be used inside\n *  and one for use outside of transactions:\n * - [TMVar.new] and [STM.newTMVar] create a new filled [TMVar]\n * - [TMVar.empty] and [STM.newEmptyTMVar] create an empty [TMVar]\n *\n * ## Reading the content of a [TMVar]\n *\n * Taking the value out of a [TMVar]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(10)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.take()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(\"Result $result\")\n *   println(\"New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-01.kt -->\n *\n * Should the [TMVar] be empty at the time of calling [STM.take], it will call [STM.retry], suspend and wait for another transaction to\n *  put a value back.\n *\n * This behaviour can be avoided by using [STM.tryTake] instead:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.tryTake()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(\"Result $result\")\n *   println(\"New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-02.kt -->\n *\n * Another effect of using either [STM.take] or [STM.tryTake] is that the [TMVar] will be empty after a successful call. Alternatively if you just\n *  want to read without emptying you can use either [STM.read] or [STM.tryRead] which will not remove the value.\n *  As with [STM.take] [STM.read] will fail and retry the transaction should the [TMVar] be empty, whereas [STM.tryTake] and [STM.tryRead] will return null instead.\n *\n ","middle":"* ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.new(30)\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.read()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(\"Result $result\")\n *   println(\"New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   val result = atomically {\n *     tmvar.tryRead()\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(\"Result $result\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-04.kt -->\n *\n * ## Setting the value of a [TMVar]:\n *\n * Changing the value of an empty [TMVar]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TMVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val tmvar = TMVar.empty<Int>()\n *   atomically {\n *     tmvar.put(20)\n *   }\n *   //sampleEnd\n *   println(\"New value ${atomically { tmvar.tryTake() } }\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-tmvar-05.kt -->\n *\n * Should the [TMVar] be full, [STM.put] will call [STM.retry] and wait for another transaction to empty the [TMVar] again.\n *  This can be avoided by using [STM.tryPut] instead. {"path":"arrow-libs/fx/arrow-fx-stm/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/fx/stm/STM.kt","prefix":"package arrow.fx.stm\n\nimport arrow.fx.stm.internal.STMTransaction\nimport arrow.fx.stm.internal.alterHamtWithHash\nimport arrow.fx.stm.internal.lookupHamtWithHash\nimport kotlin.reflect.KProperty\n\n/**\n * # Consistent and safe concurrent state updates\n *\n * Software transactional memory, or STM, is an abstraction for concurrent state modification.\n * With [STM] one can write code that concurrently accesses state and that can easily be composed without\n *  exposing details of how it ensures safety guarantees.\n * Programs running within an [STM] transaction will neither deadlock nor have race-conditions.\n *\n * > The api of [STM] is based on the haskell package [stm](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/stm) and the implementation is based on the GHC implementation for fine-grained locks.\n *\n * The base building blocks of [STM] are [TVar]'s and the primitives [retry], [orElse] and [catch].\n *\n * ## STM Datastructures\n *\n * There are several datastructures built on top of [TVar]'s already provided out of the box:\n * - [TQueue]: A transactional mutable queue\n * - [TMVar]: A mutable transactional variable that may be empty\n * - [TSet], [TMap]: Transactional Set and Map\n * - [TArray]: Array of [TVar]'s\n * - [TSemaphore]: Transactional semaphore\n * - [TVar]: A transactional mutable variable\n *\n * All of these structures (excluding [TVar]) are built upon [TVar]'s and the [STM] primitives and implementing other\n *  datastructures with [STM] can be done by composing the existing structures.\n *\n * ## Reading and writing to concurrent state:\n *\n * In order to modify transactional datastructures we have to be inside the [STM] context. This is achieved either by defining our\n *  functions with [STM] as the receiver or using [stm] to create lambda functions with [STM] as the receiver.\n *\n * Running a transaction is then done using [atomically]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transfer(from: TVar<Int>, to: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   withdraw(from, amount)\n *   deposit(to, amount)\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.deposit(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   acc.write(current + amount)\n *   // or the shorthand acc.modify { it + amount }\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.withdraw(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   if (current - amount >= 0) acc.write(current - amount)\n *   else throw IllegalStateException(\"Not enough money in the account!\")\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   val acc1 = TVar.new(500)\n *   val acc2 = TVar.new(300)\n *   println(\"Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   println(\"Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   println(\"Performing transaction\")\n *   atomically { transfer(acc1, acc2, 50) }\n *   println(\"Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   println(\"Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-01.kt -->\n * This example shows a banking service moving money from one account to the other with [STM].\n * Should the first account not have enough money we throw an exception. This code is guaranteed to never deadlock and to never\n *  produce an invalid state by committing after the read state has changed concurrently.\n *\n *  > Note: A transaction that sees an invalid state (a [TVar] that was read has been changed concurrently) will restart and try again.\n *   This usually means we rerun the function entirely, therefore it is recommended to keep transactions small and to never use code that\n *   has side-effects inside. However no kotlin interface can actually keep you from doing side effects inside STM.\n *   Using side-effects such as access to resources, logging or network access comes with severe disadvantages:\n *   - Transactions may be aborted at any time so accessing resources may never trigger finalizers\n *   - Transactions may rerun an arbitrary amount of times before finishing and thus all effects will rerun.\n *\n * ## Retrying manually\n *\n * It is sometimes beneficial to manually abort the current transaction if, for example, an invalid state has been read. E.g. a [TQueue] had no elements to read.\n *  The aborted transaction will automatically restart once any previously accessed variable has changed.\n *\n * This is achieved by the primitive [retry]:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.async\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transfer(from: TVar<Int>, to: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   withdraw(from, amount)\n *   deposit(to, amount)\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.deposit(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   acc.write(current + amount)\n *   // or the shorthand acc.modify { it + amount }\n * }\n *\n * fun STM.withdraw(acc: TVar<Int>, amount: Int): Unit {\n *   val current = acc.read()\n *   if (current - amount >= 0) acc.write(current - amount)\n *   else retry() // we now retry if there is not enough money in the account\n *   // this can also be achieved by using `check(current - amount >= 0); acc.write(it + amount)`\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * fun main(): Unit = runBlocking {\n *   val acc1 = TVar.new(0)\n *   val acc2 = TVar.new(300)\n *   println(\"Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   println(\"Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   async {\n *     println(\"Sending money - Searching\")\n *     delay(2000)\n *     println(\"Sending money - Found some\")\n *     atomically { acc1.write(100_000_000) }\n *   }\n *   println(\"Performing transaction\")\n *   atomically {\n *     println(\"Trying to transfer\")\n *     transfer(acc1, acc2, 50)\n *   }\n *   println(\"Balance account 1: ${acc1.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   println(\"Balance account 2: ${acc2.unsafeRead()}\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-02.kt -->\n *\n * Here in this (silly) example we changed `withdraw` to use [retry] and thus wait until enough money is in the account, which after\n *  a few seconds just happens to be the case.\n *\n * [retry] can be used to implement a lot of complex transactions and many datastructures like [TMVar] or [TQueue] use to to great effect.\n *\n * ## Branching with [orElse]\n *\n * [orElse] is another important primitive which allows a user to detect if a branch called [retry] and then use a fallback instead.\n *  If the fallback retries as well the whole transaction retries.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking\n * import arrow.fx.stm.atomically\n * import arrow.fx.stm.TVar\n * import arrow.fx.stm.STM\n * import arrow.fx.stm.stm\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun STM.transaction(v: TVar<Int>): Int? =\n *   stm {\n *     val result = v.read()\n *     check(result in 0..10)\n *     result\n *   } orElse { null }\n * //sampleEnd\n *\n * fun main(): Unit = runBlocking {\n *   val v = TVar.new(100)\n *   println(\"Value is ${v.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   atomically { transaction(v) }\n *     .also { println(\"Transaction returned $it\") }\n *   println(\"Set value to 5\")\n *   println(\"Value is ${v.unsafeRead()}\")\n *   atomically { v.write(5) }\n *   atomically { transaction(v) }\n *     .also { println(\"Transaction returned $it\") }\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-stm-03.kt -->\n *\n * This example uses [stm] which is a helper just like the stdlib function [suspend] to ease use of an infix function like [orElse].\n * In this transaction, when the value inside the variable is not in the correct range, the transaction retries (due to [check] calling [retry]).\n * If it is in the correct range it simply returns the value. [orElse] here intercepts a call to [retry] and executes the alternative which simply returns null.\n *\n * ## Exceptions\n *\n * Throwing inside [STM] will let the exception bubble up to either a [catch] handler or to [atomically] which will rethrow it.\n *\n * > Note: Using `try {...} catch (e: Exception) {...}` is not","middle":" encouraged because any state change inside `try` will not be undone when\n","suffix":" *   an exception occurs! The recommended way of catching exceptions is to use [catch] which properly rolls back the transaction!\n *\n * Further reading:\n * - [Composable memory transactions, by Tim Harris, Simon Marlow, Only calls to [STM.write] need to be synchronized, however the performance of [STM] is still\n *  heavily linked to the amount of [TVar]'s accessed so it is good practice to keep transactions short.\n *\n * Keeping transactions short has another benefit which comes from another drawback of [STM]:\n * There is no notion of fairness when it comes to transactions. {"path":"arrow-libs/resilience/arrow-resilience/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/resilience/CircuitBreaker.kt","prefix":"package arrow.resilience\n\nimport arrow.atomic.Atomic\nimport arrow.core.Either\nimport arrow.core.identity\nimport arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker.State.Closed\nimport arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker.State.HalfOpen\nimport arrow.resilie","middle":"nce.CircuitBreaker.State.Open\n","suffix":"import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException\nimport kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred\nimport kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable\nimport kotlinx.coroutines.withContext\nimport kotlin.time.Duration\nimport kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.nanoseconds\nimport kotlin.time.TimeMark\nimport kotlin.time.TimeSource\n\n/**\n * A [CircuitBreaker] is used to `protect` resources or services from being overloaded\n * When a service is being overloaded, interacting with it more will only worsen its overloaded state.\n * Especially when combined with retry mechanisms such as [Schedule],\n * in some cases simply using a back-off retry policy might not be sufficient during peak traffics.\n *\n * To allow such overloaded resources from overloading, [CircuitBreaker] can help you `protect` the service by failing-fast.\n * Thus [CircuitBreaker] helps us to achieve stability and prevent cascading failures in distributed systems.\n *\n * [CircuitBreaker] has three [CircuitBreaker.State]:\n *  1. [Closed]: This is its normal state, where requests are being made. The state in which [CircuitBreaker] starts.\n *    - When an exception occurs it increments the failure counter\n *    - A successful request will reset the failure counter to zero\n *    - When the failure counter reaches the [maxFailures] threshold, the breaker is tripped into the [Open] state\n *\n *  2. [Open]: The [CircuitBreaker] will short-circuit/fail-fast all requests\n *    - All requests short-circuit/fail-fast with `ExecutionRejected`\n *    - If a request is made after the configured [resetTimeout] passes, the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped into the a [HalfOpen] state, allowing one request to go through as a test.\n *\n *  3. [HalfOpen]: The [CircuitBreaker] is in this state while it's allowing a request to go through, as a `test request`\n *    - All other requests made while `test request` is still running will short-circuit/fail-fast.\n *    - If the `test request` succeeds then the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped back into [Closed], with the resetTimeout and the failures count also reset to initial values.\n *    - If the `test request` fails, then the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped back into [Open], the [resetTimeout] is multiplied by the [exponentialBackoffFactor], up to the configured [maxResetTimeout].\n *\n * Let's say we'd want to create a [CircuitBreaker] that only allows us to call a remote service twice,\n * and then whenever more than two requests fail with an exception, the circuit breaker starts short-circuiting failing-fast.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n * import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n * //sampleStart\n *   val circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker(\n *     resetTimeout = 2.seconds,\n *     openingStrategy = CircuitBreaker.OpeningStrategy.Count(maxFailures = 2),\n *     exponentialBackoffFactor = 1.2,\n *     maxResetTimeout = 60.seconds,\n *   )\n *   circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { \"I am in Closed: ${circuitBreaker.state()}\" }.also(::println)\n *\n *   println(\"Service getting overloaded . . .\")\n *\n *   Either.catch { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { throw RuntimeException(\"Service overloaded\") } }.also(::println)\n *   Either.catch { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { throw RuntimeException(\"Service overloaded\") } }.also(::println)\n *   circuitBreaker.protectEither { }.also { println(\"I am Open and short-circuit with ${it}. ${circuitBreaker.state()}\") }\n *\n *   println(\"Service recovering . . .\").also { delay(2000) }\n *\n *   circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow { \"I am running test-request in HalfOpen: ${circuitBreaker.state()}\" }.also(::println)\n *   println(\"I am back to normal state closed ${circuitBreaker.state()}\")\n * //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-circuitbreaker-01.kt -->\n *\n * A common pattern to make fault-tolerant/resilient systems is to compose a [CircuitBreaker] with a backing-off policy retry Schedule to guarantee not overloading the resource and the client interacting with it.\n * but also not the client that is interacting with the resource.\n * Below you can see how the simple `retry` function will result in `Either.Left<CircuitBreaker.RejectedExecution>`,\n * but when we combine it with another schedule, it will always call the `CircuitBreaker` on times that it could've entered the [HalfOpen] state.\n * The reason why [Schedule] is not sufficient to make your system resilient is because you also have to take into account parallel calls to your functions,\n *; In contrast, a [CircuitBreaker] can track failures of every function call or even different functions to the same resource or service.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Either\n * import arrow.resilience.CircuitBreaker\n * import arrow.resilience.Schedule\n * import arrow.resilience.retry\n * import kotlinx.coroutines.delay\n * import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds\n *\n * suspend fun main(): Unit {\n *   suspend fun apiCall(): Unit {\n *     println(\"apiCall . . .\")\n *     throw RuntimeException(\"Overloaded service\")\n *   }\n *\n *   //sampleStart\n *   val circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker(\n *     resetTimeout = 2.seconds,\n *     openingStrategy = CircuitBreaker.OpeningStrategy.Count(maxFailures = 2),\n *     exponentialBackoffFactor = 2.0, // enable exponentialBackoffFactor\n *     maxResetTimeout = 60.seconds, // limit exponential back-off time\n *   )\n *\n *   suspend fun <A> resilient(schedule: Schedule<Throwable, *>, f: suspend () -> A): A =\n *     schedule.retry { circuitBreaker.protectOrThrow(f) }\n *\n *   Either.catch {\n *     resilient(Schedule.recurs(5), ::apiCall)\n *   }.let { println(\"recurs(5) apiCall twice and 4x short-circuit result from CircuitBreaker: $it\") }\n *\n *   delay(2000)\n *   println(\"CircuitBreaker ready to half-open\")\n *\n *   // Retry once and when the CircuitBreaker opens after 2 failures then retry with exponential back-off with same time as CircuitBreaker's resetTimeout\n *   val fiveTimesWithBackOff = Schedule.recurs<Throwable>(1) andThen\n *     Schedule.exponential(2.seconds) and Schedule.recurs(5)\n *\n *   Either.catch {\n *     resilient(fiveTimesWithBackOff, ::apiCall)\n *   }.let { println(\"exponential(2.seconds) and recurs(5) always retries with actual apiCall: $it\") }\n *   //sampleEnd\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-circuitbreaker-02.kt -->\n */\n\npublic class CircuitBreaker\nprivate constructor(\n  private val state: Atomic<State>,\n  private val resetTimeout: Duration,\n  private val exponentialBackoffFactor: Double,\n  private val maxResetTimeout: Duration,\n  private val timeSource: TimeSource,\n  private val onRejected: suspend () -> Unit,\n  private val onClosed: suspend () -> Unit,\n  private val onHalfOpen: suspend () -> Unit,\n  private val onOpen: suspend () -> Unit\n) {\n\n  /** Returns the current [State], meant for debugging purposes.*/\n  public suspend fun state(): State = state.get()\n\n  /**\n   * Awaits for this `CircuitBreaker` to be [Closed].\n   *\n   * If this `CircuitBreaker` is already in a closed state, then it returns immediately,\n   * otherwise it will wait (asynchronously) until the `CircuitBreaker` switches to the [Closed] state again.\n   */\n  public suspend fun awaitClose(): Unit =\n    when (val curr = state.get()) {\n      is Closed -> Unit\n      is Open -> curr.awaitClose.await()\n      is HalfOpen -> curr.awaitClose.await()\n    }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns a new task that upon execution will execute the given task, but with the protection of this circuit breaker.\n   * If an exception in [fa] occurs, other than an [ExecutionRejected] exception, it will be rethrown.\n   */\n  public suspend fun <A> protectEither(fa: suspend () -> A): Either<ExecutionRejected, A> =\n    try {\n      Either.Right(protectOrThrow(fa))\n    } catch (e: ExecutionRejected) {\n      Either.Left(e)\n    }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns a new task that upon execution will execute the given task, but with the protection of this circuit breaker.\n   * If an exception in [fa] occurs it will be rethrown\n   */\n  public tailrec suspend fun <A> protectOrThrow(fa: suspend () -> A): A =\n    when (val curr = state.get()) {\n      is Closed -> markOrResetFailures(Either.catch { fa() })\n      is Open -> {\n        if (curr.expiresAt.hasPassedNow()) {\n          // The Open state has expired, so we are transition to HalfOpen and attempt to close the CircuitBreaker\n          if (!state.compareAndSet(curr, HalfOpen(curr.openingStrategy, curr.resetTimeout, curr.awaitClose))) protectOrThrow(fa)\n          else attemptReset(fa, curr.resetTimeout, curr.awaitClose, curr.startedAt)\n        } else {\n          // Open isn't expired, so we reject execution\n          val expiresInMillis = curr.expiresAt.elapsedNow().absoluteValue.inWholeMilliseconds\n          onRejected.invoke()\n          throw ExecutionRejected(\n            \"Rejected because the CircuitBreaker is in the Open state, attempting to close in $expiresInMillis millis\",\n            curr\n          )\n        }\n      }\n\n      is HalfOpen -> {\n        // CircuitBreaker is in HalfOpen state, which means we still reject all tasks, while waiting to see if our attempt to close the CircuitBreaker succeeds or fails\n        onRejected.invoke()\n        throw ExecutionRejected(\"Rejected because the CircuitBreaker is in the HalfOpen state\", curr)\n      }\n    }\n\n  /** Function for counting failures in the `Closed` state, triggering the `Open` state if necessary.*/\n  private tailrec suspend fun <A> markOrResetFailures(result: Either<Throwable, A>): A =\n    when (val curr = state.get()) {\n      is Closed -> {\n        when (result) {\n          is Either.Right -> {\n            val openingStrategy = state.get().openingStrategy\n            if (openingStrategy is OpeningStrategy.Count && openingStrategy.failuresCount == 0)\n              result.value\n            else {\n              if (!state.compareAndSet(curr, Closed(openingStrategy.resetFailuresCount()))) markOrResetFailures(result)\n              else result.value\n            }\n          }\n\n          is Either.Left -> {\n            val currentOpeningStrategy = curr.openingStrategy.trackFailure(timeSource.markNow())\n            // In case of failure, we either increment the failures counter, or we transition in the `Open` state.\n            if (currentOpeningStrategy.shouldOpen()) {\n              // We've gone over the permitted failures threshold, so we need to open the circuit breaker\n              val update = Open(currentOpeningStrategy, timeSource.markNow(), resetTimeout, CompletableDeferred())\n              if (!state.compareAndSet(curr, update)) markOrResetFailures<A>(result)\n              else {\n                onOpen.invoke()\n                throw result.value\n              }\n            } else {\n              // It's fine, just increment the failures count\n              if (!state.compareAndSet(curr, Closed(currentOpeningStrategy))) markOrResetFailures<A>(result)\n              else throw result.value\n            }\n          }\n        }\n      }\n\n      else -> result.fold({ throw it }, ::identity)\n    }\n\n  /** Internal function that is the handler for the reset attempt when the circuit breaker is in `HalfOpen`.\n   * In this state we can either transition to `Closed` in case the attempt was successful, or to `Open` again, in case the attempt failed.\n   *\n   * @param task is the task to execute, along with the attempt handler attached\n   * @param resetTimeout is the last timeout applied to the previous [Open] state,\n   * to be multiplied by the backoff factor in case the attempt fails, and it needs to transition to [Open] again\n   */\n  private suspend fun <A> attemptReset(\n    task: suspend () -> A,\n    resetTimeout: Duration,\n    awaitClose: CompletableDeferred<Unit>,\n    lastStartedAt: TimeMark\n  ): A = try {\n    onHalfOpen.invoke()\n    task.invoke()\n  } catch (e: CancellationException) {\n    // We need to return to Open state, otherwise we get stuck in Half-Open (see https://github.com/monix/monix/issues/1080 )\n    state.set(Open(state.get().openingStrategy ,lastStartedAt, resetTimeout, awaitClose))\n    onOpenAndThrow(e)\n  } catch (e: Throwable) {\n    // Failed reset, which means we go back in the Open state with new expiry val nextTimeout\n    val value: Duration = (resetTimeout * exponentialBackoffFactor)\n    val nextTimeout = if (maxResetTimeout.isFinite() && value > maxResetTimeout) maxResetTimeout else value\n    state.set(Open(state.get().openingStrategy, timeSource.markNow(), nextTimeout, awaitClose))\n    onOpenAndThrow(e)\n  }.also {\n    // While in HalfOpen only a reset attempt is allowed to update the state, so setting this directly is safe\n    state.set(Closed(state.get().openingStrategy.resetFailuresCount()))\n    awaitClose.complete(Unit)\n    onClosed.invoke()\n  }\n\n  private suspend fun onOpenAndThrow(original: Throwable): Nothing {\n    runCatching {\n      withContext(NonCancellable) { onOpen.invoke() }\n    }.exceptionOrNull()?.let { original.addSuppressed(it) }\n    throw original\n  }\n\n  /** Returns a new circuit breaker that wraps the state of the source\n   * and that upon a task being rejected will execute the given [callback].\n   *\n   * This is useful for gathering stats.\n   *\n   * NOTE: calling this method multiple times will create a circuit breaker that will call multiple callbacks,\n   * thus the callback given is cumulative with other specified callbacks.\n   *\n   * @param callback will be executed when tasks get rejected.\n   * @return a new circuit breaker wrapping the state of the source.\n   */\n  public fun doOnRejectedTask(callback: suspend () -> Unit): CircuitBreaker =\n    CircuitBreaker(\n      state = state,\n      resetTimeout = resetTimeout,\n      exponentialBackoffFactor = exponentialBackoffFactor,\n      maxResetTimeout = maxResetTimeout,\n      onRejected = suspend { onRejected.invoke(); callback.invoke() },\n      timeSource = timeSource,\n      onClosed = onClosed,\n      onHalfOpen = onHalfOpen,\n      onOpen = onOpen\n    )\n\n  /** Returns a new circuit breaker that wraps the state of the source\n   * and that will fire the given callback upon the circuit breaker\n   * transitioning to the [CircuitBreaker.State.Closed] state.\n   *\n   * It is useful for gathering stats.\n   *\n   * NOTE: calling this method multiple times will create a circuit\n   * breaker that will call multiple callbacks, thus the callback\n   * given is cumulative with other specified callbacks.\n   *\n   * @param callback will be executed when the state evolves into [CircuitBreaker.State.Closed].\n   * @return a new circuit breaker wrapping the state of the source.\n   */\n  public fun doOnClosed(callback: suspend () -> Unit): CircuitBreaker =\n    CircuitBreaker(\n      state = state,\n      resetTimeout = resetTimeout,\n      exponentialBackoffFactor = exponentialBackoffFactor,\n      maxResetTimeout = maxResetTimeout,\n      onRejected = onRejected,\n      timeSource = timeSource,\n      onClosed = suspend { onClosed.invoke(); callback.invoke(); },\n      onHalfOpen = onHalfOpen,\n      onOpen = onOpen\n    )\n\n  /** Returns a new circuit breaker that wraps the state of the source\n   * and that will fire the given callback upon the circuit breaker\n   * transitioning to the [CircuitBreaker.State.HalfOpen] state.\n   *\n   * It is useful for gathering stats.\n   *\n   * NOTE: calling this method multiple times will create a circuit\n   * breaker that will call multiple callbacks, thus the callback\n   * given is cumulative with other specified callbacks.\n   *\n   * @param callback is to be executed when the state evolves into [CircuitBreaker.State.HalfOpen]\n   * @return a new circuit breaker wrapping the state of the source\n   */\n  public fun doOnHalfOpen(callback: suspend () -> Unit): CircuitBreaker =\n    CircuitBreaker(\n      state = state,\n      resetTimeout = resetTimeout,\n      exponentialBackoffFactor = exponentialBackoffFactor,\n      maxResetTimeout = maxResetTimeout,\n      timeSource = timeSource,\n      onRejected = onRejected,\n      onClosed = onClosed,\n      onHalfOpen = { onHalfOpen.invoke(); callback.invoke() },\n      onOpen = onOpen\n    )\n\n  /** Returns a new circuit breaker that wraps the state of the source\n   * and that will fire the given callback upon the circuit breaker\n   * transitioning to the [CircuitBreaker.State.Open] state.\n   *\n   * It is useful for gathering stats.\n   *\n   * NOTE: calling this method multiple times will create a circuit\n   * breaker that will call multiple callbacks, thus the callback\n   * given is cumulative with other specified callbacks.\n   *\n   * @param callback will be executed when the state evolves into [CircuitBreaker.State.Open]\n   * @return a new circuit breaker wrapping the state of the source\n   */\n exponentialBackoffFactor,\n      maxResetTimeout = maxResetTimeout,\n      timeSource = timeSource,\n      onRejected = onRejected,\n      onClosed = onClosed,\n      onHalfOpen = onHalfOpen,\n      onOpen = { onOpen.invoke(); callback.invoke() }\n    )\n\n  /**\n   * The initial state when initializing a [CircuitBreaker] is [Closed].\n   *\n   * The available states are:\n   *  - [Closed] in case tasks are allowed to go through\n   *  - [Open] in case the circuit breaker is active and rejects incoming tasks\n   *  - [HalfOpen] in case a reset attempt was triggered, and it is waiting for the result in order to evolve in [Closed], or back to [Open]\n   */\n  public sealed class State {\n    public abstract val openingStrategy: OpeningStrategy\n\n    /**\n     * [Closed] is the normal state of the [CircuitBreaker], where requests are being made. - When the failure counter reaches the [maxFailures] threshold, the breaker is tripped into the [Open] state\n     *\n     * @param openingStrategy is the strategy that will decide if the circuit breaker should open after some failures.\n     */\n    public class Closed(public override val openingStrategy: OpeningStrategy) : State()\n\n    /**\n     *  When the [CircuitBreaker] is in the [Open] state it will short-circuit/fail-fast all requests\n     *    - All requests short-circuit/fail-fast with [ExecutionRejected]\n     *    - If a request is made after the configured [resetTimeout] passes, the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped into the a [HalfOpen] state, allowing one request to go through as a test.\n     *\n     * @param openingStrategy is the strategy that will awaitClose: CompletableDeferred<Unit>,\n    ) : State() {\n\n      /** The timestamp in milliseconds since the epoch, specifying when the [Open] state is to transition to [HalfOpen].\n       *\n       * It is calculated as:\n       * `startedAt + resetTimeout`\n       */\n      public val expiresAt: TimeMark = startedAt + resetTimeout\n\n      override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean =\n        if (other is Open) this.startedAt == startedAt && this.resetTimeout == resetTimeout\n        else false\n\n      override fun toString(): String =\n        \"CircuitBreaker.State.Open(startedAt=$startedAt, resetTimeoutNanos=$resetTimeout, expiresAt=$expiresAt)\"\n\n      override fun hashCode(): Int {\n        var result = startedAt.hashCode()\n        result = 31 * result + resetTimeout.hashCode()\n        result = 31 * result + expiresAt.hashCode()\n        return result\n      }\n    }\n\n    /**\n     * The [CircuitBreaker] is in [HalfOpen] state while it's allowing a test request to go through.\n     *   - All other requests made while the test request is still running will short-circuit/fail-fast.\n     *   - If the `test request` succeeds, then the [CircuitBreaker] is tripped back into [Closed], with the reset timeout, and the failures count also reset to their initial values.\n     *   - If the `test request` fails, then the [HalfOpen].\n     * If the test request failed, the [CircuitBreaker] will go back into [Open] and it'll multiply the [resetTimeout] with the exponential backoff factor.\n     */\n    public class {"path":"arrow-libs/core/arrow-core/src/commonMain/kotlin/arrow/core/Option.kt","prefix":"@file:OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)\npackage arrow.core\n\nimport arrow.core.raise.EagerEffect\nimport arrow.core.raise.Effect\nimport arrow.core.raise.SingletonRaise\nimport arrow.core.raise.option\nimport arrow.core.raise.recover\nimport kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts\nimport kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind\nimport kotlin.contracts.contract\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmName\nimport kotlin.jvm.JvmStatic\n\n/**\n * <!--- TEST_NAME OptionKnitTest -->\n *\n * If you have worked with Java at all in the past, it is very likely that you have come across a `NullPointerException` at some time (other languages will throw similarly named errors in such a case). Usually this happens because some method returns `null` when you weren't expecting it and, thus, isn't dealing with that possibility in your client code. A value of `null` is often abused to represent an absent optional value.\n * Kotlin tries to solve the problem by getting rid of `null` values altogether, and providing its own special syntax [Null-safety machinery based on `?`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/null-safety.html).\n *\n * Arrow models the absence of values through the `Option` datatype similar to how Scala, Haskell, and other FP languages handle optional values.\n *\n * `Option<A>` is a container for an optional value of type `A`. If the value of type `A` is present, the `Option<A>` is an instance of `Some<A>`, containing the present value of type `A`. If the value is absent, the `Option<A>` is the object `None`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.none\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val someValue: Option<String> = Some(\"I am wrapped in something\")\n * val emptyValue: Option<String> = none()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"value = $someValue\")\n *  println(\"emptyValue = $emptyValue\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-01.kt -->\n *\n * Let's write a function that may or may not give us a string, thus returning `Option<String>`:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(fl","middle":"ag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n","suffix":" *  if (flag) Some(\"Found value\") else None\n * //sampleEnd\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-02.kt -->\n *\n * Using `getOrElse`, we can provide a default value `\"No value\"` when the optional argument `None` does not exist:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some(\"Found value\") else None\n *\n * val value1 =\n * //sampleStart\n *  maybeItWillReturnSomething(true)\n *     .getOrElse { \"No value\" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(value1)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-03.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n * import arrow.core.getOrElse\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some(\"Found value\") else None\n *\n * val value2 =\n * //sampleStart\n *  maybeItWillReturnSomething(false)\n *   .getOrElse { \"No value\" }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(value2)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-04.kt -->\n *\n * Checking whether option has value:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * fun maybeItWillReturnSomething(flag: Boolean): Option<String> =\n *  if (flag) Some(\"Found value\") else None\n *\n *  //sampleStart\n * val valueSome = maybeItWillReturnSomething(true) is None\n * val valueNone = maybeItWillReturnSomething(false) is None\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main() {\n *  println(\"valueSome = $valueSome\")\n *  println(\"valueNone = $valueNone\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-05.kt -->\n * Creating a `Option<T>` of a `T?`. Useful for working with values that can be nullable:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val myString: String? = \"Nullable string\"\n * val option: Option<String> = Option.fromNullable(myString)\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"option = $option\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-06.kt -->\n *\n * Option can also be used with when statements:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val someValue: Option<Double> = Some(20.0)\n * val value = when(someValue) {\n *  is Some -> someValue.value\n *  is None -> 0.0\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-07.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val noValue: Option<Double> = None\n * val value = when(noValue) {\n *  is Some -> noValue.value\n *  is None -> 0.0\n * }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"value = $value\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-08.kt -->\n *\n * An alternative for pattern matching is folding. This is possible because an option could be looked at as a collection or foldable structure with either one or zero elements.\n *\n * One of these operations is `map`. This operation allows us to map the inner value to a different type while preserving the option:\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.None\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val number: Option<Int> = Some(3)\n * val noNumber: Option<Int> = None\n * val mappedResult1 = number.map { it * 1.5 }\n * val mappedResult2 = noNumber.map { it * 1.5 }\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"number = $number\")\n *  println(\"noNumber = $noNumber\")\n *  println(\"mappedResult1 = $mappedResult1\")\n *  println(\"mappedResult2 = $mappedResult2\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-09.kt -->\n * Another operation is `fold`. This operation will extract the value from the option, or provide a default if the value is `None`\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.Option\n * import arrow.core.Some\n *\n * val fold =\n * KNIT example-option-11.kt -->\n *\n * Arrow also adds syntax to all datatypes so you can easily lift them into the context of `Option` where needed.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.some\n * import arrow.core.none\n *\n * //sampleStart\n *  val some = 1.some()\n *  val none = none<String>()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"some = $some\")\n *  println(\"none = $none\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-12.kt -->\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.toOption\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val nullString: String? = null\n * val valueFromNull = nullString.toOption()\n *\n * val helloString: String? = \"Hello\"\n * val valueFromStr = helloString.toOption()\n * //sampleEnd\n * fun main () {\n *  println(\"valueFromNull = $valueFromNull\")\n *  println(\"valueFromStr = $valueFromStr\")\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-13.kt -->\n *\n * You can easily convert between `A?` and `Option<A>` by using the `toOption()` extension or `Option.fromNullable` constructor.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * import arrow.core.firstOrNone\n * import arrow.core.toOption\n * import arrow.core.Option\n *\n * //sampleStart\n * val foxMap = mapOf(1 to //sampleStart\n *    Some(1).map { it + 1 }\n *  //sampleEnd\n *  println(value)\n * }\n * ```\n * <!--- KNIT example-option-15.kt -->\n *\n * ## Credits\n *\n * Contents partially adapted from [Scala Exercises Option Tutorial](https://www.scala-exercises.org/std_lib/options)\n * Originally based on the Scala Koans.\n */\npublic sealed class Option<out A> {\n\n  public companion object {\n\n    @JvmStatic\n    public fun <A> fromNullable(a: A?): Option<A> = if (a != null) Some(a) else None\n\n    @JvmStatic\n    public operator fun <A> invoke(a: A): Option<A> = Some(a)\n\n    @JvmStatic\n    @JvmName(\"tryCatchOrNone\")\n    /**\n     * Ignores exceptions and returns None if one is thrown\n     */\n    public inline fun <A> catch(f: SingletonRaise<None>.() -> A): Option<A> {\n      contract { callsInPlace(f, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) }\n      return catch({ None }, f)\n    }\n\n    @JvmStatic\n    @JvmName(\"tryCatch\")\n    public inline fun <A> catch(recover: (Throwable) -> Option<A>, f: SingletonRaise<None>.() -> A): Option<A> {\n      contract {\n        callsInPlace(f, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)\n        callsInPlace(recover, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)\n      }\n      return recover({ f(SingletonRaise(this)).some() }, { None }, recover)\n    }\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * The given function is applied as a fire and forget effect\n   * if this is a `None`.\n   * When applied the result is ignored and the original\n   * None value is returned\n   *\n   * Example:\n   * ```kotlin\n   * import arrow.core.Some\n   * import arrow.core.none\n   *\n   * fun main() {\n   *   Some(12).onNone { println(\"flower\") } // Result: Some(12)\n   *   none<Int>().onNone { println(\"flower\") }  // Result: prints \"flower\" and returns: None\n   * }\n   * ```\n   * <!--- KNIT example-option-16.kt -->\n   */\n  public inline fun onNone(action: () -> Unit): Option<A>  {\n    contract {\n      callsInPlace(action, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)\n    }\n    return also { if (it.isNone()) action() }\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * The given function is applied as a fire and forget effect\n   * if this is a `some`.\n   * When applied the result is ignored and the original\n   * Some value is returned\n   *\n   * Example:\n   * ```kotlin\n   * import arrow.core.Some\n   * import arrow.core.none\n   *\n   * fun main() {\n   *   Some(12).onSome { println(\"flower\") } // Result: prints \"flower\" and returns: Some(12)\n   *   none<Int>().onSome { println(\"flower\") }  // Result: None\n   * }\n   * ```\n   * <!--- KNIT example-option-17.kt -->\n   */\n  public inline fun onSome(action: (A) -> Unit): Option<A>  {\n    contract {\n      callsInPlace(action, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)\n    }\n    return also { if (it.isSome()) action(it.value) }\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns true if the option is [None], false otherwise.\n   * @note Used only for performance instead of fold.\n   */\n  public fun isNone(): Boolean {\n    contract {\n      returns(false) implies (this@Option is Some<A>)\n      returns(true) implies (this@Option is None)\n    }\n    return this@Option is None\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns true if the option is [Some], false otherwise.\n   * @note Used only for performance instead of fold.\n   */\n  public fun isSome(): Boolean {\n    contract {\n      returns(true) implies (this@Option is Some<A>)\n      returns(false) implies (this@Option is None)\n    }\n    return this@Option is Some<A>\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns true if this option is nonempty '''and''' the predicate\n   * $p returns true when applied to this $option's value.\n   * Otherwise, returns false.\n   *\n   * Example:\n   * ```kotlin\n   * import arrow.core.Some\n   * import arrow.core.None\n   * import arrow.core.Option\n   *\n   * fun main() {\n   *   Some(12).isSome { it > 10 } // Result: true\n   *   Some(7).isSome { it > 10 }  // Result: false\n   *\n   *   val none: Option<Int> = None\n   *   none.isSome { it > 10 }      // Result: false\n   * }\n   * ```\n   * <!--- KNIT example-option-18.kt -->\n   *\n   * @param predicate the predicate to test\n   */\n  public inline fun isSome(predicate: (A) -> Boolean): Boolean {\n    contract {\n      callsInPlace(predicate, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)\n      returns(true) implies (this@Option is Some<A>)\n    }\n    return this@Option is Some<A> && predicate(value)\n  }\n\n  /**\n   * Returns the encapsulated value [A] if this instance represents [Some] or `null` if it is [None].\n   *\n   * ```kotlin\n   * import arrow.core.None\n   * import arrow.core.Some\n   * import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe\n   *\n   * fun test() {\n   *   Some(12).getOrNull() shouldBe 12\n   *   None.getOrNull() shouldBe null\n   * }\n   * ```\n   * <!--- KNIT example-option-19.kt -->\n A [Saga] is useful when you need to manage data in a consistent manner\n * across services in distributed transaction scenarios. Or when you need to compose multiple\n * `actions` with a `compensation` that needs to run in a transaction like style.\n *\n * For example, let's say that we have the following domain types `Order`, `Payment`.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * data class Order(val id: UUID, val amount: Long)\n * data class Payment(val id: UUID, val orderId: UUID)\n * ```\n *\n * The creation of an `Order` can only remain when a payment has been made. In SQL, you might run\n * this inside a transaction, which can automatically roll back the creation of the `Order` when the\n * creation of the Payment fails.\n *\n * When you need to do this across distributed services, or a multiple atomic references, etc. You\n * need to manually facilitate the rolling back of the performed actions, or compensating actions.\n *\n * The [Saga] type, and [saga] DSL remove all the boilerplate of manually having to facilitate this\n * with a convenient suspending DSL.\n *\n * ```kotlin\n * data class Order(val id: UUID, val amount: Long)\n * suspend fun createOrder(): Order = Order(UUID.randomUUID(), 100L)\n * suspend fun deleteOrder(order: Order): Unit = println(\"Deleting $order\")\n *\n * data class Payment(val id: UUID, val orderId: UUID)\n * suspend fun createPayment(order: Order): Payment = Payment(UUID.randomUUID(), order.id)\n * suspend fun deletePayment(payment: Payment): Unit = println(\"Deleting $payment\")\n *\n * suspend fun Payment.awaitSuccess(): Unit = throw RuntimeException(\"Payment Failed\")\n *\n * suspend fun main() {\n *   saga {\n *     val order = saga({ createOrder() }) { deleteOrder(it) }\n *     val payment = saga { createPayment(order) }, ::deletePayment)\n *     payment.awaitSuccess()\n *   }.transact()\n * }\n * ```\n */\npublic typealias Saga<A> = suspend SagaScope.() -> A\n\n/** DSL that enables the For example, it is\n * fine to `filter` by `name` and then increase the `age`,\n * but not to `filter` by `name` and then capitalize the `name`.\n *\n * In general terms, this optic does not satisfy the rule that\n * applying two modifications in a row is equivalent to\n * applying those two modifications at once. The following\n * example shows that increasing by one twice is not equivalent\n * to increasing by two.\n *\n * ```\n * val p = Optional.filter<Int> { it % ","middle":"2 == 0 }  // focus on even null\n *\n * p.modify(n) { it + 2 }\n * // ------------------- = 4\n * ```\n *\n * The reader interested in a (deep) discussion about why\n * this rule is important may consult the blog post\n * It is especially useful when multiple resources that depend on each other need to be acquired and later released in reverse order.\n * The capability of _installing_ resources is called [ResourceScope], and [Resource] defines the value associating the `acquisition` step, and the `finalizer`.\n * [Resource] allocates and releases resources in a safe way that co-operates with you want to compose other `suspend` functionality into resource safe programs, such as concurrency, parallelism or Arrow's Effect.\n *\n * Creating a [Resource] _value_ can be done using the signal, or an exception is received during `acquire`, the resource is assumed to not have been acquired and thus will not trigger the release function.\n *  => Any composed resources that are already AcquireStep\n\n@ResourceDSL\npublic interface ResourceScope : AutoCloseScope {\n\n  /**\n   * Compose another [Resource] program into this [ResourceScope].\n   * All [release] functions [install]ed into the [Resource] lambda will be installed in this [ResourceScope] while respecting the FIFO order.\n   */\n  @ResourceDSL\n  public suspend fun <A> Resource<A>.bind(): A\n  /**\n   * Install [A] into the [ResourceScope].\n   * Its [release] function will be called with the appropriate [ExitCase] if this [ResourceScope] finishes.\n   * It results either in [ExitCase.Completed], [ExitCase.Cancelled] or [ExitCase.Failure] depending on the terminal state of [Resource] lambda.\n   */\n  @ResourceDSL\n  public suspend fun <A> install(\n    acquire: suspend AcquireStep.() -> A,\n    release: suspend (A, ExitCase) -> Unit,\n  ): A\n\n  /** Composes a [release] action to a [Resource] value before binding. */\n  @ResourceDSL\n  public suspend infix fun <A> Resource<A>.release(release: suspend (A) -> Unit): A {\n    val a = bind()\n    return install({ a }) { aa, _ -> release(aa) }\n  }\n\n  /** Composes a [releaseCase] action to a [Resource] value before binding. */\n  @ResourceDSL\n  public suspend infix fun <A> Resource<A>.releaseCase(release: suspend (A, ExitCase) -> Unit): A {\n    val a = bind()\n    return install({ a }, release)\n  }\n\n ResourceScope.() -> A): Resource<A> = block\n\n/**\n * The [resourceScope] function creates the [ResourceScope] instances,\n * runs the user [action] while allocating the _installed_ resources.\n *
